blocks.text: All the six trigonometric functions repeat their values for each increase or decrease of \(2\pi\) in \(\theta\); therefore, the values of trigonometric functions for \(\theta\) and \(\theta \pm 2n\pi\), where \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\), are the same. This behaviour of trigonometric functions is called periodicity.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Think of the days of the week: after every 7 days the same day comes again. On the unit circle, adding \(2\pi\) to an angle is one complete turn, so the terminal side comes back to the same point \(P(x, y)\). The same point gives the same \(x\) and \(y\), hence the same values of all six functions:
\[\sin(\theta + 2\pi) = \sin\theta, \quad \cos(\theta - 4\pi) = \cos\theta\]

Period of a trigonometric function is the smallest \(+ve\) number which, when added to the original circular measure of the angle, gives the same value of the function. A function is periodic if \(f(\theta + p) = f(\theta)\), for all \(\theta\) in the domain of the function, and the least positive value of \(p\) is called the period of the function.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two conditions are packed into this definition:
1. \(f(\theta + p) = f(\theta)\) must hold for every \(\theta\), not just for one angle.
2. Among all such positive numbers \(p\), the period is the least one. For sine, \(2\pi\), \(4\pi\) and \(6\pi\) all repeat the values, but the period is \(2\pi\).
Now, let us discover the periods of the trigonometric functions.
Theorem 11.1: Sine is a periodic function and its period is \(2\pi\).

Proof: Suppose \(p\) is the period of sine function such that
\[\sin(\theta + p) = \sin\theta \quad \text{for all } \theta \in \mathbb{R} \quad \text{(A)}\]
Now put \(\theta = 0\), we have
\[\sin(0 + p) = \sin 0\]
\[\Rightarrow \sin p = 0\]
\[\Rightarrow p = 0, +\pi, +2\pi, +3\pi, \ldots\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why put \(\theta = 0\)? Equation (A) has to hold for every \(\theta\), so it must hold in particular for \(\theta = 0\). This gives a short list of candidates for \(p\): the numbers with \(\sin p = 0\), i.e. the multiples of \(\pi\). The period has to be one of them; we only have to test which is the smallest one that works for every \(\theta\).
\(p = 0\) is dropped at once, because a period must be positive.

(i) If \(p = \pi\), then from (A)
\[\sin(\theta + \pi) = \sin\theta \quad \text{(not true)}\]
\[\because \sin(\pi + \theta) = -\sin\theta\]
Thus \(\pi\) is not the period of \(\sin\theta\).
(ii) If \(p = 2\pi\), then from (A)
\[\sin(\theta + 2\pi) = \sin\theta, \quad \text{which is true}\]
\[\because \sin(0 + 2\pi) = \sin 0\]
As \(2\pi\) is the smallest positive real number for which \(\sin(\theta + 2\pi) = \sin\theta\), \(2\pi\) is the period of \(\sin\theta\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does \(p = \pi\) fail? Adding \(\pi\) is half a turn: \(P(x, y)\) goes to the opposite point \((-x, -y)\), so the sine changes sign. For example \(\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\) but \(\sin\frac{3\pi}{2} = -1\). One counter-example is enough to reject \(\pi\).
Why does \(p = 2\pi\) work for every \(\theta\)? Adding \(2\pi\) is a full turn, which brings every point back to itself; the book checks the case \(\theta = 0\), and the same reason holds for all \(\theta\). Since the only candidates were \(\pi, 2\pi, 3\pi, \ldots\) and \(\pi\) failed, \(2\pi\) is the smallest.
Theorem 11.2: Tangent is a periodic function and its period is \(\pi\).

Proof: Suppose \(p\) is the period of tangent function such that
\[\tan(\theta + p) = \tan\theta \quad \text{for all } \theta \in \mathbb{R} \quad \text{(B)}\]
Now put \(\theta = 0\), we have
\(\tan(0 - p) = \tan 0\) \(\Rightarrow \tan p = 0\)
\[p = 0, \pi, 2\pi, 3\pi, \ldots\]
(i) If \(p = \pi\), then from (B) \(\tan(\theta + \pi) = \tan\theta\), which is true.
As \(\pi\) is the smallest positive number for which \(\tan(\theta + \pi) = \tan\theta\),
therefore, \(\pi\) is the period of \(\tan\theta\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: After putting \(\theta = 0\) in (B), the book prints \(\tan(0 - p) = \tan 0\). It should be \(\tan(0 + p) = \tan 0\), which gives \(\tan p = 0\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is \(\tan(\theta + \pi) = \tan\theta\) true? Half a turn changes the signs of both sine and cosine, and the two minus signs cancel:
\[\tan(\theta + \pi) = \dfrac{\sin(\theta + \pi)}{\cos(\theta + \pi)}\]
\[= \dfrac{-\sin\theta}{-\cos\theta} = \tan\theta\]
So tangent repeats after only half a turn, which is why its period \(\pi\) is half that of sine.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text:
By adopting the procedure used in finding the periods of sine and tangent, we can prove that
(i) \(2\pi\) is the period of \(\cos\theta\)
(ii) \(2\pi\) is the period of \(\csc\theta\)
(iii) \(2\pi\) is the period of \(\sec\theta\)
(iv) \(\pi\) is the period of \(\cot\theta\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
A quick rule that follows from Example 1 (our summary, useful for checking): for a number \(a \ne 0\),
\[\text{period of } \sin ax, \cos ax = \dfrac{2\pi}{|a|}\]
\[\text{period of } \tan ax, \cot ax = \dfrac{\pi}{|a|}\]
Adding a constant does not change the period. In an exam, still show the working as in Example 1.

blocks.title: Example 1
steps:
Given: (i) \(\sin 2x\); (ii) \(3 + \tan\frac{x}{3}\).
To find: the period of each function, i.e. the smallest positive number which, added to \(x\), gives the same value.
Method: use the known periods (\(2\pi\) for sine, \(\pi\) for tangent) and rewrite the shifted angle so that the change in \(x\) itself can be read off.

Step 1: (i) Use the period of sine
\[\sin(2x + 2\pi) = \sin 2x\]
Why: the period of sine is \(2\pi\), so adding \(2\pi\) to the angle \(2x\) (whatever it is) gives the same value.

Step 2: (i) Take the common factor 2
\[\sin(2x + 2\pi) = \sin 2(x + \pi)\]
\[\Rightarrow \sin 2(x + \pi) = \sin 2x\]
Why: the period is about the change in \(x\), not in \(2x\). Writing \(2x + 2\pi = 2(x + \pi)\) shows that the value of \(\sin 2x\) repeats when \(x\) is increased by \(\pi\).

Step 3: (i) Conclude
Hence \(\pi\) is the period of \(\sin 2x\).
Why: \(2\pi\) is the smallest shift of the angle \(2x\) that repeats sine, so \(\pi\) is the smallest shift of \(x\). For instance, the smaller shift \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) gives \(\sin 2(x + \frac{\pi}{2}) = \sin(2x + \pi) = -\sin 2x\), not the same value.

Step 4: (ii) Consider only the tangent part
To find the period of \(3 + \tan\frac{x}{3}\), consider only \(\tan\frac{x}{3}\).
Why: the constant \(3\) is added to every value; it moves the whole graph up but cannot change when the values repeat.

Step 5: (ii) Use the period of tangent
\[\tan\left(\frac{x}{3} + \pi\right) = \tan\frac{x}{3}\]
\[\Rightarrow \tan\frac{1}{3}(x + 3\pi) = \tan\frac{x}{3}\]
Why: the period of tangent is \(\pi\), so we add \(\pi\) to the angle \(\frac{x}{3}\). Then \(\frac{x}{3} + \pi = \frac{x}{3} + \frac{3\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{3}(x + 3\pi)\).

Step 6: (ii) Conclude
The value of \(\tan\frac{x}{3}\) repeats when \(x\) is increased by \(3\pi\). Hence the period of \(3 + \tan\frac{x}{3}\) is \(3\pi\). The addition of the constant number \(3\) to the tangent function does not affect the period.
Why: \(\pi\) is the smallest shift of the angle \(\frac{x}{3}\) that repeats tangent, so \(3\pi\) is the smallest shift of \(x\).

Check:
(i) At \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\): \(\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\); at \(x = \frac{\pi}{4} + \pi\): \(\sin\frac{5\pi}{2} = 1\). Same value.
(ii) At \(x = \pi\): \(3 + \tan\frac{\pi}{3} = 3 + \sqrt{3}\); at \(x = 4\pi\): \(3 + \tan\frac{4\pi}{3} = 3 + \sqrt{3}\). Same value.
blocks.answer: (i) The period of \(\sin 2x\) is \(\pi\). (ii) The period of \(3 + \tan\frac{x}{3}\) is \(3\pi\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the solution of part (ii) the line after "We know that the period of tangent is \(\pi\)" is printed jumbled (the "=" signs and fractions overlap). It should read \(\tan\left(\frac{x}{3} + \pi\right) = \tan\frac{x}{3} \Rightarrow \tan\frac{1}{3}(x + 3\pi) = \tan\frac{x}{3}\), as in Step 5 above.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Periodicity: the values repeat; \(f(\theta + p) = f(\theta)\) for all \(\theta\). The period is the least positive such \(p\).
2. Periods: \(\sin, \cos, \csc, \sec\): \(2\pi\); \(\tan, \cot\): \(\pi\).
3. Method of proof: put \(\theta = 0\) to find the candidates, then test the smallest positive candidate for every \(\theta\).
4. \(\sin ax\) has period \(\frac{2\pi}{|a|}\); \(\tan ax\) has period \(\frac{\pi}{|a|}\); an added constant does not change the period.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Giving tangent the period \(2\pi\). \(2\pi\) does repeat tangent, but \(\pi\) is smaller, so the period is \(\pi\).
2. For \(\sin 2x\), answering \(2\pi\) or \(4\pi\). The angle \(2x\) runs twice as fast, so the period is halved: \(\pi\).
3. Thinking the constant in \(3 + \tan\frac{x}{3}\) changes the period. It only shifts the values up.
